Vasco da Gama was a Portuguese explorer who established the first direct sea route from Europe to Asia by sailing around Africa, arriving in India in 1498. His voyage opened a new era of European maritime dominance and trade, bypassing the overland Silk Road routes and allowing Portugal to establish a lucrative Asian spice empire that would define the early decades of the Age of Exploration.

King Manuel I of Portugal commissioned da Gama to find a sea route to Asia, following earlier Portuguese expeditions that had been slowly exploring Africa's coastline. He sailed south and east around Africa, rounding the Cape of Good Hope in 1488—first achieved by Bartolomeu Dias—then crossed the Indian Ocean to reach Calicut on India's southwest coast in 1498. The voyage took approximately ten months from Portugal to India. The return voyage took even longer, with crew suffering from scurvy and tropical disease.

His voyage opened direct trade between Europe and Asia, allowing Portuguese merchants to bypass Muslim middlemen in the Mediterranean and Red Sea trade routes. When he returned to Portugal in 1499, he was received as a hero, establishing Portugal's supremacy in the Asian spice trade. The profits from this monopoly funded Portuguese expansion for decades. Da Gama made two subsequent voyages to India, using military force to establish Portuguese trading posts and dominance over regional powers. His success inspired both admiration and fear—European rivals raced to find alternative routes to Asia, while local rulers viewed Portuguese encroachment with increasing alarm.
